title: How Much Deposit Should a Contractor Ask For?
description: How much deposit a contractor should ask for: typical 10 to 33 percent, state caps, and a fair milestone payment schedule.

cover.alt: Illustration of a stack of coins on a for pros blueprint background with a measuring tape

keywords: how much deposit should a contractor ask for
takeaways: In states with no cap, most contractors ask for 10 to 25 percent down, per Angi, with one third as a common ceiling.
California caps a home improvement down payment at $1,000 or 10 percent of the price, whichever is less.
Tie every payment after the deposit to finished work the client can see, and hold the final payment for the punch list.
body:
Ask for a deposit that covers your spot on the schedule and your first material order, and no more than your state allows. In states with no legal cap, Angi puts the usual range at 10 to 25 percent of the job price, and one third is a common ceiling in capped states. In California the legal cap on a home improvement job is $1,000 or 10 percent of the contract price, whichever is less, so the right answer changes with your state.

## The rule that beats every rule of thumb: check your state first

There is no single national deposit rule in the US. Deposit limits are set state by state, and a few states set no cap at all. That means a deposit that is normal in one state can be illegal in the next one over.

| State or situation | Deposit cap or usual range | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| California home improvement | $1,000 or 10 percent of price, whichever is less | CSLB |
| Massachusetts home improvement over $1,000 | No more than one third of price, unless special-order material costs more | Mass. AG guidance |
| Maryland and Virginia | Around 33 percent of contract price | Angi |
| States with no cap | Usually 10 to 25 percent asked | Angi |

California is the strictest case. The Contractors State License Board (CSLB) states the down payment should never exceed 10 percent of the contract price or $1,000, whichever is less, and CSLB home improvement contract guidance says there are no exceptions for special-order materials. The one narrow exception CSLB lists is a contractor with a blanket performance and payment bond on file, which is rare. Massachusetts, by contrast, allows a deposit up to the greater of one third of the price or the actual cost of special-order or custom material that must be ordered early.

Before you set a deposit on a contract, check your state licensing board or consumer protection office for your current cap. Rules change, contract types differ, and service and repair work, new construction and commercial work may sit under different rules than home improvement work. When in doubt, ask for less and collect the rest through progress payments. You stay legal in every state that way.

## Worked example: a $24,000 bathroom remodel

Say the signed price is $24,000. Here is the same job under three deposit setups.

- At 10 percent: $24,000 x 0.10 = $2,400 deposit
- At 20 percent: $24,000 x 0.20 = $4,800 deposit
- At one third: $24,000 / 3 = $8,000 deposit
- In California on this job: the cap is $1,000, because $1,000 is less than 10 percent ($2,400)

Now build the rest as progress payments tied to work the client can see. This schedule uses the 10 percent deposit and sums back to the full price.

| Payment | Due when | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deposit | At signing | $2,400 |
| Progress 1 | Demo done and rough plumbing in | $4,800 |
| Progress 2 | Inspection passed and drywall up | $7,200 |
| Progress 3 | Tile and fixtures set | $6,000 |
| Final | Punch list done and final walk passed | $3,600 |
| Total |  | $24,000 |

Check the sum: $2,400 + $4,800 + $7,200 + $6,000 + $3,600 = $24,000. The deposit is 10 percent, and no payment runs ahead of finished work by much. On a small job the math flips in California: on a $6,000 paint job, 10 percent is $600, which is less than $1,000, so $600 is the cap there. Use our [free estimate template](/blog/free-estimate-template/) to put this schedule in writing on the quote itself, so the client sees the full plan before signing.

## How to pick your deposit percent

Start with what the deposit has to do. It should hold the start date, cover the first material order and show the client is serious. It does not need to fund the whole job. Your progress payments do that work.

Small, short jobs often carry a higher percent because the first material order is most of the cost. A $3,000 door and trim job might need $1,200 of material on day one. Long remodels carry a lower percent and more progress payments, because risk spreads over weeks of visible work. Custom or special-order material is the one case where a larger early payment can be fair, and even then you should name the item and its cost in the contract rather than folding it into a big general deposit.

Keep two habits. First, never ask for full payment before work starts, and treat any request above 50 percent as a problem, yours or theirs. Angi warns homeowners that more than 50 percent up front is a red flag, and clients read your deposit as a trust signal. Second, take the deposit by check or card, not cash only. A paper trail protects both sides if a dispute starts. Pair the deposit with clear terms in your [painting estimate](/blog/painting-estimate-calculator/) or general estimate: start date, payment schedule, and what happens if either side cancels.

## What if a client pushes back on the deposit?

Explain what it covers in one sentence: the start date, the first material order and the crew time you turn away from other work. Then show the full schedule. Most pushback fades when clients see that the bulk of the money follows finished work, not dates.

If a client wants zero down on a material-heavy job, offer a split: a small booking deposit now, then the material payment when the order is placed and you share the supplier invoice. You stay close to your costs without asking the client to fund work they cannot see yet. Put every version in the written contract and have both sides sign any change. Verbal side deals are where deposit disputes start.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a normal deposit for a contractor?
In states with no cap, 10 to 25 percent of the job price is the usual range, per Angi. One third is a common legal ceiling in capped states such as Massachusetts, Maryland and Virginia. Small material-heavy jobs can run higher as a percent, since the first order is most of the cost.

### What is the maximum deposit in California?
For home improvement contracts, $1,000 or 10 percent of the contract price, whichever is less, per the CSLB. On a $24,000 job the cap is $1,000. On a $6,000 job the cap is $600.

### Can I ask for 50 percent down?
Only if your state allows it and the job truly needs it, such as a large special-order material bill named in the contract. As a default it hurts trust: Angi flags requests over 50 percent as a red flag for homeowners, and several states cap deposits well below that.

### Should the deposit be refundable?
State your terms in the contract before you take the money. A common fair setup refunds the deposit minus any special-order material already bought and any design or permit work already done, if the client cancels before the start date.

### When should the final payment be due?
When the job is complete and the punch list is done, not on a calendar date. Holding 10 to 15 percent for the final walk is normal: on a $24,000 job that is $2,400 to $3,600 held to the end.
